prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, opening the field of moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the pattern of discovery I find most convincing: a concrete theoretical prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) that a specific twist angle gives flat bands, followed seven years later by a clue from nature that answered it, with correlated insulators and superconductivity appearing where the theory said to look. It then did more than confirm the prediction. It created a tunable platform, with twist angle, gating and screening as control knobs, that many independent groups have reproduced, and it has spawned a large field that now extends to other moire materials. The sequence of prediction, surprise and wide replication makes it a discovery in the sense the committee cares about, and it comes with a manageable attribution story built on two prediction authors and one experimental leader. Having heard colleagues, I accept that optical lattice clocks (B024) are the cleanest candidate on attribution and maturity, and I would be content to see that prize first if the committee decides the moire interpretation needs more time. I still rank B003 slightly higher because it opened a field of new physics, while the clocks, superb as they are, are a quantitative leap in an existing field.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the central scientific question, the mechanism of superconductivity and the nature of the correlated states, remains open, so we would be honouring a platform and a phenomenon more than an understood effect. The attribution is also imperfect: Yuan Cao, the first author of the 2018 papers, and other early experimental groups fall outside the three-name limit, and the committee could well judge that to be unfair. If the committee wants a settled discovery with a clean two-person credit and a path to a practical redefinition of the second, B024 is the more defensible choice.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest case of a new measurement technique that changes what can be observed, strongly confirmed by many labs, with a clean two-person credit (Katori and Ye) and timely given the discussion of redefining the second.
responses.response: I agree with you on attribution and maturity, and on that score B024 beats my own first choice. My hesitation is about what kind of discovery it is. It sharpens a quantity we already measured, while the moire materials gave us a new phenomenon nobody had seen. I also note that the Hall and Hansch comb prize and the ion-clock prize mean the committee must show what is new in the neutral-atom lattice. Your argument that 10^-18 performance, relativistic geodesy and constant tests are new capabilities is fair, and I rank B024 just below B003 rather than dismissing it, and I would not resist it as the first prize.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked B003 fourth and says the field is young, the superconducting mechanism is unsettled, and the recognition may be premature; he also suggests a two-senior-figures configuration without Bistritzer.
responses.response: I take the prematurity point seriously and it is my main worry as well. But a Nobel Prize has not required a mechanism, only a discovery that is robust and reproduced, and the insulating and superconducting phases are firmly reproduced by many groups. I disagree with dropping Bistritzer. He is the first author of the decisive 2011 paper, and a prize that credits MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero only would blur the logic of prediction followed by discovery that makes this case attractive. If the committee has to cut the number, I would prefer to wait than to remove the prediction's first author.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B024 first, but she places B003 third and says that omitting Bistritzer is a real attribution cost and that the origin of the superconductivity makes interpretation less settled than for the other candidates.
responses.response: We agree on Bistritzer, and I would put it more strongly: with him the credit follows the intellectual structure of the discovery. Where we differ is on weight. You treat the open mechanism as a reason for caution, and I treat it as a sign of a living field, but I accept that this makes B003 a riskier choice than the clocks. I also concede your point that Dean, Young, Yazdani and Efetov, and Cao as first author, show that the experimental credit is wider than Jarillo-Herrero alone, and I do not have a full answer to that beyond the three-name limit.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks B024 first and B035 (IceCube) second, valuing patient control of systematics and a new observational window, and treats IceCube credit as more contested than the clocks.
responses.response: I share your respect for IceCube; it is the observational discovery I ranked third, and I like that nature is the source of the clue. But I agree with your own caution that the credit is contested across AMANDA, DUMAND and a large collaboration, and the astrophysical sources are still only partly identified, so the discovery is mature but the interpretation is young. In that respect it faces the same maturity question as B003 and a harder attribution question, which is why I place it behind the moire prize. I am ready to be persuaded if the experts say Halzen, Karle and Spiering are an uncontroversial trio.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics (B001) first as a genuine invention that opened sub-angstrom imaging, with a coherent Rose-Haider-Urban configuration.
responses.response: I agree that it is a real invention with a clean three-person story, and it is mature. My reservation is the category: its value is as an instrument, and its impact is through other people's science in materials and chemistry, whereas B003 is itself a discovery about nature. Pearce also notes that Krivanek's STEM corrector is outside the names, which leaves a real credit gap. I would not oppose it as a second part in a two-part prize if the numbers of names could be kept to three, but I would not choose it ahead of B003 or B024.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the superconducting mechanism in twisted graphene as a necessary maturity condition or as a normal open follow-up question.

Whether the three-name limit can be reconciled with the experimental credit for Yuan Cao and other early groups, and whether outside experts would call Jarillo-Herrero's group the decisive experiment.
Whether B024 should be taken first on grounds of attribution and maturity, with B003 waiting a few years for the mechanism to clarify.
A two-part prize combining B003 and B024 would exceed three people in total with the supplied names, so I cannot propose it within the rules.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My PhD supervisor David Gross and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet are not credited in any shortlisted ballot, and none of the credited names is at Uppsala as far as the provided profile shows.
